```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(vcdinteractive)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
```

```{r numbers, include = FALSE}
ag <- prop.table(margin.table(UCBAdmissions, c(1, 2)), 2)["Admitted", ]
agg <- mosaic_cells(margin.table(UCBAdmissions, c(2, 1)))
cond <- mosaic_cells(UCBAdmissions, expected = ~ Admit * Dept + Gender * Dept)
mc <- attr(cond, "model")
sig <- significant_cells(cond, adjust = "holm")
rate_A <- prop.table(UCBAdmissions[, , "A"], 2)["Admitted", ]
noA <- attr(mosaic_cells(UCBAdmissions[, , -1],
                         expected = ~ Admit * Dept + Gender * Dept), "model")
```

## The data

In 1973 the graduate division of the University of California, Berkeley,
was suspected of gender bias in admissions (Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell,
1975). The data for the six largest departments are in base R as
`datasets::UCBAdmissions`, a $2 \times 2 \times 6$ table
(`Admit` $\times$ `Gender` $\times$ `Dept`) with
`r sum(UCBAdmissions)` applicants.

```{r}
ftable(UCBAdmissions, row.vars = "Dept", col.vars = c("Gender", "Admit"))
```

All the plots below are interactive. You can drag the variables to change
their order, hover the tiles, and switch the residuals in the side panel.

## 1. The aggregated table

Summing over departments, `r pct(ag["Male"])` of men and
`r pct(ag["Female"])` of women were admitted. Under independence of `Gender`
and `Admit` all four cells are significant: the adjusted standardized
residuals are $\pm$ `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(agg$standardized[1]))`. Women
look under-represented among the admitted.

```{r aggregate}
imosaic(~ Gender + Admit, data = UCBAdmissions,
        main = "Aggregated over departments: Gender x Admit", height = 500)
```

## 2. Within departments

The hypothesis of no discrimination corresponds to the log-linear model
[AD][GD]: admission and gender are *conditionally* independent given the
department. Its expected counts reproduce the Dept $\times$ Admit and
Dept $\times$ Gender margins, so each department keeps its own admission rate
and its own share of women.

```{r conditional}
imosaic(~ Dept + Gender + Admit, data = UCBAdmissions,
        expected = ~ Admit * Dept + Gender * Dept,
        main = "Model [AD][GD]: Admit independent of Gender given Dept",
        height = 620)
```

The model gives $G^2 =$ `r sprintf("%.1f", mc$G2)` on `r mc$df` df. The
only significant cells (Holm correction) are the four cells of department A:

```{r}
sig
```

In department A women are admitted **more** often than men
(`r pct(rate_A["Female"])` vs `r pct(rate_A["Male"])`). Without department A
the model fits well ($G^2 =$ `r sprintf("%.1f", noA$G2)`, df = `r noA$df`,
p = `r sprintf("%.2f", noA$p_G2)`).

Try dragging `Dept` to the last position. You then see, within each gender,
how the applicants are spread over the departments.

Now **untick `Dept`** in the toolbar. The table is collapsed over the
departments and the model [AD][GD] becomes the independence of `Admit` and
`Gender`: the plot turns into the aggregated mosaic of Section 1, with its
four strongly significant cells. Tick `Dept` again and each tile splits back
into its departments. Switching between the two views shows Simpson's paradox
directly.

## 3. Why the aggregate is misleading

The department is associated with both gender and admission. Women applied
mostly to departments C–F, which admit few applicants. Men applied mostly to
A and B, which admit most of them. Aggregating over this confounder creates an
association against women that does not exist within departments, where, if
anything, women are favoured: this is Simpson's paradox.

```{r margins}
imosaic(~ Dept + Gender, data = UCBAdmissions,
        main = "Who applies where: Dept x Gender", height = 480)
imosaic(~ Dept + Admit, data = UCBAdmissions,
        main = "Admission rate by department: Dept x Admit", height = 480)
```

## Reference

Bickel, P. J., Hammel, E. A. and O'Connell, J. W. (1975). Sex bias in
graduate admissions: data from Berkeley. *Science*, 187, 398–404.
